items.docs: Pass a PostFeed, a BlogList or your own list as children. Give searchAction for a plain GET form, or onSearch inside a Client Component; it also gets an empty string when the field is cleared, so reset your list there. Set --sticky-top to your header's height, for example className="[--sticky-top:4rem]".

items.description: A three-column documentation page: your sidebar, the article with breadcrumbs and meta, and an on-this-page rail that tracks your place.
items.docs: Give every heading in children an id that matches an entry in toc. Plain h2, h3, p, ul, ol, pre and table elements are styled for you; long URLs and keys break instead of widening a phone, and a table wider than the screen scrolls on its own (give it tabIndex={0}). items.description: The body of a site search page: result count, type filters with counts as links, results with path and marked snippet, and pagination.

items.docs: Pass sections with nested pages; an entry without href is a group and renders as text. Two levels read best: anything deeper folds into a details element, and open: true keeps the branch of the current page open. Rows carry no dates on purpose. Pass labels to translate the counts and the date, and linkAs={Link} for your router. items.docs: Every card carries the same four lines, so people can compare kinds of data. Each right links to where it is used, such as a settings page or a form. Pass icons from the icons item as nodes. policyHref is required: the summary always points to the full policy and never replaces it. Pass labels to translate the four line labels and the footer. items.title: Key dates list
items.description: Term dates, deadlines and closures as a clear list of dates and ranges, with the next one marked in words.
items.docs: Dates are calendar days, sorted by their first day; a range is written once with both ends in time elements. Pass today as an ISO date for stable rendering, otherwise the current day in timeZone is used. groupBy is month, term (each date names its term) or none, and calendar is a slot for an Add to calendar link on each row. A day-first locale such as en-GB writes 24 Dec, a month-first one Dec 24. labels translates the markers. items.title: Support and SLA table
items.description: What support you get on each plan: priority levels, first response and target resolution times, channels and hours, in a real table.
items.docs: Write times the way people say them ("1 hour", "Next business day") and say in notes whether they run in business or calendar hours. A plan's rows follow the order of priorities, and null says the plan does not cover that priority. Set hours once, or per plan. The table becomes one card per plan below 768px for two plans, 1024px for three and 1280px for more, so nothing hides in a horizontal scroll. labels translates the row and column labels.

items.title: Code of conduct
items.description: A community code of conduct people will read: the promise, expected and unacceptable behaviour in pairs, how to report, and what happens next.
items.docs: Give each behaviour a title and a one-line example. report.contact is the first link after the promise, so it is easy to find in a bad moment: an https link opens in a new tab and shows an arrow, a mailto or tel link stays plain. Every section and every behaviour has an anchor (#conduct-reporting); set idPrefix when a page holds two codes. scope says where the code applies, and labels translates the headings. The layout follows the width of its column, not the screen: the two lists sit side by side from 672px and the three reporting facts from 896px, so the contact never breaks across lines.

items.name: press-release-list
items.title: Press release list
items.description: Your own announcements by year: headline, date and optional PDF per row, with the company boilerplate and the media contact in sticky cards beside them.
items.docs: Pass releases with an ISO dateTime: the year groups and the order (newest first) come from it, and a dateTime with a time is filed under the year it falls in timeZone, the same day the row shows. date is the short form shown in the row; leave it out and dateTime is written with locale. A release without pdfHref has no download link, and the PDF link is named by what it fetches: Download, the headline, PDF and the size. The boilerplate and contact cards are optional and sit beside the list from 1024px, held in view below --sticky-top (6rem by default; set it to the height of your sticky header) on screens at least 46rem tall, so a short laptop screen never cuts them off; without them the list takes the full width. Only the copy button is a client component, so the block works in a Server Component. Pass labels to translate the fixed words and linkAs={Link} to route the release links.

items.name: roadmap-columns
items.title: Roadmap columns
items.description: A public roadmap in Now, Next and Later columns: each item with a status in words and a short why, and no dates you cannot keep.
items.docs: Pass three or four columns. A column with the id now, next, later or shipped also gets that phase's mark in its heading; any other id can pass phase. A card with an href is one stretched link and a card without one stays plain. Write statuses in words (In progress, Designing, Exploring) and keep dates out: that is the point. Each column is a labelled list with its count in the heading, and the cards of every lane start on one line from 768px. shippedHref adds a link to your changelog under the board, and note replaces the built-in Plans change footnote (pass null to leave it out). Pass linkAs={Link} to route the card links.

items.name: pay-bands-table
items.title: Pay bands table
items.description: Published salary bands by role family and level, with a zone switch, a bar for each range and a plain note on how pay is set.
items.docs: bands are keyed by zone id; a level without a band in the chosen zone says so in words. The bars share one scale across every zone, so they move when the zone changes, and the two ends of the scale are written in the Range heading. Pass zone and onZoneChange to control the switch, or defaultZone to start on another zone; with a single zone the switch is left out. Amounts are written from currency and locale without decimals. List the levels from the first rung up. On a phone each bar sits under its level so the table fits; one that is still too wide scrolls inside its own container with the level column held in place. notes takes the facts about the rest of the package (bonus, equity, review cycle) and methodology a plain paragraph on how bands are set.

items.title: Subprocessor list
items.description: The vendors that process customer data for you: purpose, data, location and transfer safeguard, sorted and dated, with a slot for the notify-me form.
items.docs: Rows are sorted alphabetically for you. location takes one country or several, always as names, never a flag alone. The notice slot is yours: put the notify-me form or a line on how changes are announced there. items.name: accessibility-statement
items.title: Accessibility statement
items.description: The accessibility statement a site must publish: conformance in the heading, known gaps with workarounds and dates, how you tested and who to tell.
items.docs: status is written into the heading as words (fully conforms, partially conforms, does not conform), so it never relies on a badge or a colour. Pass assessed with a dateTime so the date is a time element, and keep it honest: test again after every redesign and update the date. limitations={[]} states that there are none, and leaving it out drops the section. fixBy takes a string or the dated object. Pass labels to translate the headings and the heading sentence.

items.name: document-library
items.title: Document library
items.description: Downloadable documents grouped by category: format, size, pages, language and date on every row, real download links and optional search.
items.docs: Every Download is a plain anchor with the download attribute, and its name reads Download, then the title, the type and the size. Pass filename when the saved name should differ from the file on the server. searchable adds a field that filters by title, description, type and language and announces how many documents are left. Dates follow locale, and a date without a time is never shifted. Downloads are not routes, so there is no linkAs. The block is a client component because of the search: use it from a Server Component with plain data. labels are plain strings too, with {query}, {shown}, {total} and {noun} as placeholders, so they can cross from a Server Component.

items.name: video-library
items.title: Video library
items.description: A library of talks, demos and tutorials: 16:9 cards with a duration chip, speaker and date, grouped by playlist, as links or buttons for your own player.
items.docs: duration is written m:ss or h:mm:ss: it is shown as given, spoken in full by the card's link name (12 minutes 4 seconds) and added up into the playlist's total. thumbnail is a 16:9 picture URL; without one the card shows the first letter of the title. featured lets the first video lead the first playlist: two columns, and from 1024px two rows when the playlist has three or more videos (a playlist of three fills that block exactly). With onPlay the cards are buttons and href is ignored, so use that from a Client Component. A playlist without videos says so. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the links.

items.name: class-timetable
items.title: Class timetable
items.description: A weekly timetable for a gym, school or studio: the week at a glance on wide screens, a day at a time on a phone, with spots left and full classes in words.
items.docs: Pass days with Monday first, each with its classes (start and end on the 24-hour clock; 9:30 and 09:30 both work, and the classes are listed by the clock). The week is a grid once the timetable itself is 64rem wide, about 9rem a day; narrower, and in a narrow column on a wide screen, day tabs open on today. today is the id of the current day: work it out for your visitor's time zone, or leave it out and nothing is marked. spots: 0 flags a class as Full in words and with a dashed edge, and waitlistHref adds the waitlist link only then, named after its class for screen readers (labels.waitlistFor words that). locale decides how times are written: en-US 6:30 PM, en-GB 18:30. A range that does not fit its card wraps after the dash. legend is a line under the timetable. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the class links.

items.name: service-area-list
items.title: Service area list
items.description: The places you work, as links to local pages in balanced columns grouped by region, with a radius note and an Other places line.
items.docs: Places are sorted for you: alphabetically, or largest first when places carry a priority (any number, a population works). A place without an href is plain text, so no link goes nowhere. radius is two parts, label and from, joined into one sentence. The Other places line shows when contactHref is set; labels changes its words. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the place links.

items.name: directions-by-mode
items.title: Getting here
items.description: How to arrive by train, bus, car, bike and on foot, with routes that start at the station, a facts line for each and a step-free access panel.
items.docs: Pass the address, a mapHref and the modes in the order people use them. Each mode has a kind (train, bus, car, bike, walk, ferry or plane) that picks its icon, a title that names it in words, and a body: one paragraph, or an array for numbered steps. Write every route from the place people start, with stop names, line numbers and the last 200 metres, and wrap those in strong. facts are label and value pairs such as the journey time from a named origin and the parking cost; link adds a timetable or parking-map link, routed with linkAs. access is the separate panel for step-free entry, lifts, accessible parking and assistance dogs: its points are sentences, or a short label with its sentence. From 1024px it stays in view beside the routes while they scroll past; set --sticky-top on the section to the height of a sticky header you have (2rem by default). The icons that have a motion play it when a row is hovered or focused and stay still for reduced motion. Pass labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: allergen-matrix
items.title: Allergen matrix
items.description: Every dish against the fourteen EU allergens in a sticky-header table, with chips that hide dishes containing what you cannot eat.
items.docs: Pass dishes with a course and the ids of the allergens they contain and may contain. The columns are the fourteen EU allergens by default (EU_ALLERGENS, exported from the allergens file); pass allergens to use another list, each with an id, a full name and an optional short name for the narrow column head. A cell says Contains or May contain in words for screen readers and draws a solid disc or a ring, so colour is never the signal. The chips are a toggle group: value, defaultValue and onValueChange control which allergens are picked. Dishes that contain a picked allergen are hidden, and so are dishes that may contain it unless the reader switches that off (defaultHideMayContain starts it on). The count is announced as the list changes. The first column and the header row stay in place inside the scrolling table, and a soft shade on the right and bottom edge shows while there is more behind it; set --matrix-max-height (40rem by default) to change how tall it gets before it scrolls. legend, updated and note sit under the table. Pass labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: founder-letter
items.title: Founder letter
items.description: A letter from the person behind the company: dated, addressed to the reader, set for reading and signed with name, role and portrait.
items.docs: Pass the date (a label and an ISO dateTime), the place, a salutation and the paragraphs as children: plain p, ul, ol, blockquote, strong and a elements are styled, so Markdown output works as it is. signoff is the line before the signature and signer is a name, a role and a portrait URL; initials stand in until the portrait loads or when it fails. postscript is inline content that gets a paragraph of its own and is never collapsed; links and strong in it are styled like the body. title adds a subject line (an h2 unless you set headingLevel). The column is 38rem wide at a generous line height, and nothing about it is decorative. Pass labels to change the words that open the postscript.

items.name: values-rows
items.title: Values rows
items.description: Company values as hairline rows: the value in large type, its meaning in a sentence, and a concrete We do and We do not pair.
items.docs: Pass an eyebrow, a title and three to six values. Each value needs a name, a one-sentence meaning, and one behaviour for does and one for doesNot, each checkable in a day at work; the component asks for the pair so a bare list is not possible. A value with an href gets a link under its pair, set with labels.more and routed with linkAs. Rows are an ordered list with an index, and stack on a phone with the name first. The two columns carry their own icon and words, so neither relies on colour. headingLevel is the section title's level; the value names sit one below it.

items.name: topic-hub
items.title: Topic hub header
items.description: The top of a topic page: description, a fact strip, a numbered Start here reading path and related topics as chips.
items.docs: title is the topic's name and the page's h1 by default; set headingLevel to 2 when the page already has one (the Start here panel and the related topics sit one level below). facts are label and value pairs: articles, contributors, a time element for the last update. startHere takes three to five pieces with a title, href, reading time in minutes and a line about them; it is an ordered list, so the sequence is announced, and each row is one stretched link. related are chips that link to their own hubs, with an optional count that is read out in words. children is placed under the related topics for the latest articles or a newsletter form. items.name: key-takeaways
items.title: Key takeaways
items.description: A summary box for the top of a long article: three to five takeaways, reading time, intended audience and up to three jump links.
items.docs: Pass three to five points, short enough to read in ten seconds. minutes, audience and jumps fill the footer; give it any of them, and up to three jumps are shown, each an anchor to a section of the article. The box is a section labelled by its own heading (title, an h2 unless you set headingLevel), so assistive technology lists it as a landmark and can skip to it or past it. That is the difference from Callout, which is not a landmark. Pass labels to translate the reading time, the audience words and the jump label.

items.name: article-series-outline
items.title: Series outline
items.description: Where you are in a multi-part series: every part in order, with Read, You are here and Soon told in words, as a card or a strip.
items.docs: Pass the series (a title and an optional href) and the parts in order. current is the number of the page you are on, counted from 1; leave it out on the series' own page. A part before it is Read, the current one is You are here and carries aria-current, and a part after it is plain text marked Soon, with its releaseDate when it has one, unless it has an href: then it is a published part and links. Set state on a part to override that, for a site that knows what each reader has read. layout is card (a sidebar, or the end of an article beside the pager) or strip (across the top of the body); both follow the width of their own column. Upcoming parts are never dead links. The outline is a navigation landmark named after the series; give two outlines on one page their own aria-label. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the links and labels to translate the words.

items.name: interview-layout
items.title: Interview layout
items.description: A Q&A article with questions set apart from answers, a sticky guest card and room for pull quotes between exchanges.
items.docs: Pass the guest (a name, role, portrait, a line about them and links) and the exchanges. Each exchange is one item of an ordered list with the question as a heading, so a reader can jump from question to question; answer is a string (one paragraph), an array (one paragraph each) or your own markup, and quote is a string attributed to the guest or an object that names another speaker. The guest card is sticky beside the questions from 1024px (set --sticky-top to the height of your sticky header) and sits above the first question on a phone. title, eyebrow, intro, interviewer, date and readingTime make up the header, and children follows the last answer. Pass labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: version-support-table
items.title: Version support table
items.description: Which versions you still support: release date, end of active support, end of life and a status in words, with the next change flagged.
items.docs: Pass versions with a name, an ISO released date, activeUntil and securityUntil, and optionally a status (current, supported, security-only or end-of-life) and a notesHref. Without a status it is worked out from the dates; Current is always your call. A date that has passed says Ended, and the one date across the table that will change a status next is flagged where it sits, so colour is never the only signal. Dates are written year first by default (dateFormat iso) and sit in time elements; dateFormat medium writes them with locale. Pass a fixed today for stable rendering and tests; without it the current day in timeZone is used. Below 768px each version becomes a card that keeps every label. note sits under the table for what active support and security fixes mean. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the release-notes links.

items.name: open-source-credits
items.title: Open source credits
items.description: The libraries your product ships, with version and licence, searchable and linked to each full licence text in a dialog.
items.docs: Pass packages (a name, version, SPDX license and optional repository) and licenseTexts keyed by SPDX id. Packages are grouped by licence family, so BSD-2-Clause and BSD-3-Clause sit together, with a count for each, and sorted by name within a licence. A licence with a text opens it in a dialog with a button that copies it, for a notice file; a browser that refuses to copy gets the text selected instead. The dialog joins the line breaks of hand-wrapped paragraphs so the text reads on a phone; the button copies it exactly as you supplied it. A licence without a text is shown as plain words, an empty licence reads Unknown, and a dual licence such as MIT OR Apache-2.0 opens either text. The search field filters by package name and announces how many are left; searchable={false} drops it for a short list. licenseFamily and licenseParts are exported from the licenses file. Supply the real text of each licence: it carries each project's own copyright line. Pass labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: incident-postmortem
items.title: Incident postmortem
items.description: A blameless post-incident report: severity in words, impact in tabular figures, a UTC timeline, the root cause in plain words and actions with owners.
items.docs: Pass the incident (id, title, severity as critical, major or minor with an optional code such as SEV 2, start and end as ISO times, what was affected, and a summary that can be several paragraphs), the impact (figures with a label, a number or text, and a note, plus a body), the timeline (events with a time, text and an optional milestone word such as Detected, Mitigated or Resolved), the rootCause (a one-sentence summary, an explanation and contributing factors), the lessons (wentWell and wentPoorly) and the actions (title, owner, due date and status as done, in-progress or planned, with an optional ticket and link). Blameless by design: owners are teams, and a person is shown only when you pass person. Every section has an anchor and a link beside its heading, so #timeline sends a customer straight to the timeline; idPrefix keeps the anchors apart when a page holds more than one report. All times are written in one zone, UTC by default (timeZone), with the time since the start beside each event, a day label when the incident spans midnight, and a duration worked out from the two ends or Ongoing when there is no end. A contents list follows the reader beside the page on wide screens and becomes a row of links on a phone; the actions table becomes cards below 768px. Events are sorted by time, numbers are tabular, and linkAs routes the ticket links. Pass labels to translate every fixed word and note to change or remove the blameless line.

items.name: incident-postmortem-demo
items.title: Incident postmortem demo
items.description: A working preview of Incident postmortem.

items.name: recipe-layout
items.title: Recipe layout
items.description: A recipe page that cooks well: times and servings up front, ingredients that rescale, large-numeral steps with timers and a nutrition panel.
items.docs: Pass title, intro, times (prep, cook and total in minutes; the total is worked out when left out), servings (the number the quantities are written for), ingredients (quantity, unit, name, note, with unitPlural and plural for words that change, and group for a heading such as For the sauce), steps (text, an optional image and an optional timer in minutes), nutrition per serving, tips and onServingsChange. The stepper rescales every quantity the way a cook writes it: halves, thirds and quarters as fractions (1½ tbsp), grams and millilitres to the nearest 5 once they are big and as kilograms and litres past a thousand, 3 tsp as 1 tbsp, and a line without a quantity never scales. Set whole on an ingredient such as eggs to keep it a whole number. The new count is announced, and an amount that changes lights up for a moment. Steps are an ordered list with large numerals; a timer counts down in place against the clock, can be paused and reset, and is announced when it starts and ends; Start gives way to Pause and Reset brings Start back, with focus handed on so the keyboard keeps its place. Where the browser has the Wake Lock API a Keep screen awake switch appears; set keepAwake to false to remove it. The ingredients stay in view beside the steps from 1024px and come first on a phone. For search engines, structuredData writes schema.org Recipe data into the page from the same props (pass true, or an object with image, author, cuisine, category, datePublished and keywords); recipeJsonLd() in recipe-layout/schema gives you the same object to place yourself, written for the servings the recipe is written for. Pass labels and locale for another language.

items.name: article-footnotes
items.title: Article footnotes
items.description: Footnote references and a notes list with working back links, so a long article can cite sources without breaking the flow.
items.docs: Wrap the article in Footnotes with a list of notes, each with a stable id, its content and optionally a source (label, href and the day you read it). Put FootnoteRef note="id" in the text where a claim needs one and FootnoteList wherever the notes belong, usually at the end. A reference takes its number from the place of its note in the list, so numbers follow the list while the anchors (#fn-id for a note, #fnref-id for the spot in the text) keep working when notes are added or moved. Following a reference puts focus on the note, which is also highlighted when a link targets it; the back link returns focus to the exact sentence. A note that is cited twice sets mentions to 2, and the second FootnoteRef passes mention=2. Notes use the muted colour at 14px or larger, with the source line in the foreground colour. Pass labels, title and backLabel to translate the fixed words, and locale for the date.

items.name: newsletter-card
items.title: Newsletter card
items.description: A compact subscribe card for sidebars and article ends: a line of promise, one field, one button and a note on frequency.
items.docs: Pass title, description, onSubmit (resolve to confirm, reject to show the error), promise, cta, privacyHref and compact. The card is built to be 20rem wide in a sidebar and lays out in two columns when it is wide, because it follows its own width rather than the screen's. The address is checked in words before anything is sent. A failure keeps what was typed and turns the button into a retry; success replaces the form with a message that says what happens next, takes focus and is announced, and offers to start again. Compact leaves out the icon and the description for a footer column. value, defaultValue and onValueChange control the field; defaultStatus starts the card in success or error for a page that already knows the result. items.name: sticky-cta-bar
items.title: Sticky CTA bar
items.description: A bar fixed to the bottom that appears once the hero has scrolled away, with the product, a price or promise and one action; it can be dismissed.
items.docs: Pass label, description, action and, when it should appear, showAfter: a number of pixels from the top, or the id of an element (usually the hero) that has to scroll out of view first. hideWhen is the id of an element, such as the footer or a sign-up form, that hides the bar for as long as any part of it is on screen. The bar watches both with IntersectionObserver, so there is no scroll handler. It slides in with a short transform that becomes a fade for people who prefer less motion, floats as a card from 640px and is a full-width strip on a phone, keeps clear of the safe area, and is out of the tab order and the accessibility tree whenever it is hidden. While it shows it adds room at the bottom of the page and a scroll padding, so it never covers the last lines or a focused field. dismissible adds a labelled close button, onDismiss is called, and storageKey remembers the choice for the browser session; closed from the keyboard, focus goes back to the element it came from. Inside a preview frame, a dialog or any pane that scrolls instead of the window, pass that element as scrollRoot (a ref): the bar is then positioned inside it rather than fixed to the screen.

items.name: pricing-rows
items.title: Pricing rows
items.description: Plans as stacked rows: name and pitch on the left, price in the middle, action on the right, for four tiers or more.
items.docs: Pass plans (id, name, pitch, limits, price, period, action and featured), a title and a note. A numeric price is written as money in currency and locale and counts to its new value; text such as Free or Custom is shown as written. Give price and period as objects keyed by monthly and yearly and a billing toggle appears; control it with interval and onIntervalChange, or let it run itself from defaultInterval, and put yearlySaving beside the yearly option. A plan that gives only one interval keeps it for both. Switching is announced once. The featured plan gets a badge (its text can be changed per plan) and a heavier outline. The layout follows its own width: four columns when it is wide, name and limits beside price and action in the middle, and name, pitch, limits, price and action stacked on a phone, with full-width buttons. The action is any element, normally a Button; give the featured plan the solid one, and give each action an accessible name that includes its plan, such as aria-label="Start 14-day trial, Team plan", so a list of buttons does not read the same words several times. The names are headings one level below the title.

items.name: contact-form-centered
items.title: Centered contact form
items.description: A narrow, centred contact form with a topic select, a message and a clear promise of when you will answer, for sites that need one simple way in.

Mistakes are said in words next to the field, only once the reader has been in that field or has tried to send, and the first one takes focus. Sending disables the button but keeps its label. A failure keeps everything typed and hands focus back to the button. Success replaces the form with a status message that repeats the address it will answer and the promise, takes focus and is announced; Send another message starts again at the name field. messageLimit sets the counter, defaultValues pre-fills what you already know, and defaultStatus starts the form in the invalid, error or done state for a page that already knows it. The heading reads the period first, 30 days, full refund, no questions; write {period} inside the title to put it elsewhere, or word the whole heading yourself. The seal is drawn inline from concentric rings, a milled edge and a check, takes the page's colours in both themes and is hidden from assistive technology, so the promise reads without it. items.title: Trial timeline
items.description: A free trial told day by day: what you get today, when you are reminded and what happens at the end, so nobody wonders if they will be charged.

The moments are an ordered list: a row when the section is wide and a column when it is narrow, decided by the width of the section itself, so it holds in a sidebar as well as on a phone. The connecting line is decoration and hidden from assistive technology. The last moment is the answer to what happens at the end, so it is emphasised by weight, a filled marker and a heavier title, never by colour. Without an icon a moment shows its step number. items.title: Talk to us CTA
items.description: A closing ask led by real people: faces, names and roles, a first-person heading, two actions and a status dot with words for how fast they reply.
items.docs: Pass one to three people (a name, a role and an optional photo), a title written in the first person, an optional description, the actions, an availability line and a status of online, away or offline. The faces overlap on a ring in the card colour and are hidden from assistive technology because the names are written below them; three names share one row in three equal columns, so none is left alone on a second line. Status is a dot and words together: the dot is solid when online, a ring when away and a thin ring when offline, and the availability text must say the state too, for example Online now, replies in about 10 minutes. The line is a polite status region, so a change is announced once and nothing is read on load. The actions stack on a phone and sit side by side when there is room. items.title: Audience discounts
items.description: Startups, students and nonprofits: a card per group with who qualifies, how much off as the biggest figure and how to apply, so nobody has to ask.
items.docs: Pass a title, two to four programs, an optional description and a note about how you check. A program is an id, the audience, the discount, an optional duration, the eligibility as a list of lines, an action and an optional icon. The discount is real text set as the biggest thing on the card, with the duration under it; eligibility is a list so it can be scanned; the action is an object with a label that names the group, such as Apply for the student discount, and either an href or an onClick, and it renders as a link or a button accordingly. Cards are articles in a list, and the columns follow the count so no card is left alone in a row: two groups stay a pair, three go from one column to three, four from two to four, and a single one stays a card. The cards share their rows through a subgrid, so the figures, the dividers, the lists and the buttons line up from one card to the next, and the buttons fill the row so they are equally tall. items.name: office-list
items.title: Office list
items.description: Every office with address, phone, email and hours, with an open-now line worked out in each office's own time zone and the zone said in words.
items.docs: Pass the offices (an id, a city, an optional name, the address as lines, a phone, an email, an IANA time zone, the hours, a directions link and an optional map), a title and a layout of list or tabs. Hours are ranges of days with an opening and a closing time on the 24-hour clock in the office's own zone; a second range for the same days is a lunch break, and a day with no range is closed. A day with two ranges shows them one under the other, each on a line that never breaks, so no time is ever split across lines at any width. The open-now line, the highlighted weekday and the local time are worked out after the page has mounted, because the server does not know the reader's clock, so the markup always matches; until then the line is empty and nothing jumps. Every office also says its time zone in words, using the generic name so it never changes with daylight saving. The status reads Open now, until 18:00 or Closed, opens at 09:00, tomorrow or on a named weekday. The address, phone and email share one address element, the phone is a tel link and the email a mailto link. The list layout shows every office at once as rows; the tabs layout shows one at a time with its map beside the details. Pass now to pin the lines for a test, locale for weekday names and the zone name, and labels to translate every fixed word. The week is built here and not with OpeningHours, on purpose: it needs two ranges in a day, a zone for each office and a clock that is known only after mount, where OpeningHours takes finished text and a day index from you.

items.name: newsletter-lists
items.title: Newsletter lists
items.description: Let people choose what they get: several lists as checkbox cards with frequency, one email field and a button that says how many lists it subscribes to.
items.docs: Pass the lists (an id, a name, one line, how often and an optional defaultChecked), an onSubmit that receives the address and the ids of the chosen lists, a title and an optional description, privacyHref and minSelected. Nothing is checked unless a list is marked defaultChecked, which is what consent rules ask for. Each list is a real checkbox in a card that outlines when chosen, with the frequency beside the name. With fewer than minSelected chosen the button is off and a hint says why; once enough are chosen the hint becomes a count, and because it is a polite status region the change is announced. The button says how many lists it will subscribe to. The address is checked in words before anything is sent, a failure keeps the choices and the address, turns the button into a retry and puts focus on it, and success replaces the form with a status message that repeats the chosen lists and takes focus so a screen reader reads it. defaultStatus error or done, with defaultEmail and the lists marked defaultChecked, shows the failure or the confirmation for a page that already knows the result; labels translates every fixed word and sentence. The cards are not CheckboxCards, on purpose: the check sits on the left beside the name and the frequency is a chip next to it, where CheckboxCards puts the check on the right and has no frequency.

items.name: thank-you-next-steps
items.title: Thank-you next steps
items.description: The page after a conversion: the confirmation, what happens next in order with timings, a copyable reference, and one or two things to do while waiting.
items.docs: Pass a title that repeats what was done, a summary with the detail that matters, the steps (a label, an optional detail and when it happens), the follow-up actions and an optional reference such as a booking or order number. The title and summary are announced once when the page loads: a live region that is already full on arrival is not read, so a hidden polite status region is filled after mount. The reference is selectable and has a copy button that confirms in words and says so to a screen reader; if the browser refuses, a line says to copy it by hand and a screen reader hears it too. headingLevel goes from 1 to 4: use 1 when this block is the main content of the thank-you page. Steps are an ordered list joined by a hairline, with the timing as a chip that sits beside the step on a wide section and under it on a narrow one. The check mark is decoration. Name the reference through labels.reference, for example Booking reference or Order number; labels also translates the other fixed words. The block is not ResultState, on purpose: a thank-you page needs a page-level heading, ordered steps with timings and an announcement after mount, where ResultState is a centred panel with one description.

items.name: early-access-form
items.title: Early access form
items.description: A beta application that sorts the waitlist by fit: work email, role, team size and one optional sentence, with an invite code behind a link.
items.docs: Pass onSubmit, the roles (a value and a label each, shown in the house select), the sizes (shown as a segmented control, so keep them short), a title, an optional description and a reviewTime such as We review applications every Friday. Work email, role and team size are required; what would you use it for is optional. A mistake is said in words beside its field once the reader has been there or tried to send, and the first one takes focus. The team size row carries its name, its invalid state and its sentence like every other field, and its rail turns destructive. The I have an invite code link reveals a code field and moves focus into it, and I do not have a code takes the field away again and gives focus back to the link, so a keyboard reader never loses their place; pass checkInviteCode to check it on the way out, and a code that does not work is a sentence under the field that keeps the rest of the form as it is, while a code that works skips the queue and the confirmation says so. onSubmit may be async: the button shows busy, a rejection keeps everything typed, shows the failure and puts focus back on the button, which is the retry, and success replaces the form with a status message that says what happens next and when and takes focus. defaultValues and defaultStatus done or invited show a state for a page that already knows it; labels translates every fixed word and error.

Prices are real text in tabular figures and the duration is a visible fact. The you provide panel, access, content and a decision-maker, is what makes it a service package rather than a software plan; it is joined into a sentence in the locale you pass. One package can be marked featured, which gets a stronger border and a badge. The cards share their rows through a subgrid, so the prices, the durations, the dividers, the deliverables, the panels and the buttons line up from one card to the next, even when one price note runs to two lines, and the columns follow the count so no package is left alone in a row. items.name: refer-a-friend
items.title: Refer a friend
items.description: Customers invite friends: the deal in plain words, three steps, a personal link to copy, share options and a live count of invites, joins and credit.
items.docs: Pass the offer (what the friend gets and what the customer gets, as text), the customer's link, their stats (invited, joined and the credit earned so far, formatted by you), the terms (a link and a line on when credit arrives, both required) and an optional onShare that receives copy, email or native. The heading, the three steps and the share message are written from the offer unless you pass your own title, steps or message. The link sits in a read-only field that selects on focus, with a copy button that confirms in words and says so to a screen reader, and says it to a screen reader too when the browser refuses. The field wraps the link instead of cutting it, on a phone as on a wide panel, so the personal part at its end is always readable; on a narrow section the button sits under the field at full width. The email action is a mailto link with the message and link filled in, and the device's share sheet is offered only where the browser has one, which is known after mount so the markup always matches. The three tallies are a description list in tabular figures with their labels, and locale formats the counts. On a wide section the offer and the steps sit beside the link panel; on a narrow one they stack. labels translates every fixed word, the default steps and the share message. The default steps and message are generic (a first purchase, a first payment); pass your own steps and message to tell one story, such as a first month and a next invoice. The field is not CopyField, on purpose: it needs a link that wraps, words you can translate and a read-only field that selects itself.

items.name: ticket-tiers
items.title: Ticket tiers
items.description: Ticket types for an event with price, inclusions, how many are left and when the price rises, with sold out and not on sale yet designed as states.
items.docs: Pass the tiers (an id, a name, an optional description, the price in whole units, what is included, an optional remaining count, an optional saleStart and saleEnd as ISO times and an optional max per order), onSelect, and the currency, locale and timeZone prices and dates are written in. A tier that is sold out, ended or not on sale yet keeps its place with a disabled button and a clear label. An open tier shows how many are left, in the heavy style at or below lowStock, the date the price rises as a time element, a quantity stepper with the total, and a button that says how many tickets it buys. The stepper stops at the stock and at the limit per order; pressing plus at a limit keeps the button focusable and says why in words in a polite status line, which is also where the limit is stated before anyone hits it. Sale windows are judged on the reader's clock after mount, or on the now you pass. Until the clock is known, a tier that has a sale window shows as checking: no badge, a muted price and a disabled button that says Checking availability, so the server never renders a tier open that the browser would close. Pass now from the server and nothing is ever checking. A tier with no sale window is open straight away, and a sold-out one is sold out whatever the clock says. The badge has a row of its own above the name on every card, so names and descriptions line up however long a date is. The cards share their rows through a subgrid, so the prices, lists and buttons line up. The stepper is its own and not NumberInput, on purpose: its plus stays focusable at a limit and says why in words, where NumberInput disables its buttons and keeps them out of the tab order. labels translates the fixed words, Checking availability included.

items.name: credit-packs
items.title: Credit packs
items.description: One-off credit packs with the price per credit and the saving against the smallest pack worked out from your numbers, and one pack marked best value.
items.docs: Pass the packs (an id, credits, price in whole units and an optional label, smallest first), onSelect, and the currency and locale prices are written in. The saving and the best value badge are worked out from the packs, never typed in: the smallest pack is the standard rate, every other pack shows what it saves per credit against it, rounded down so the claim is never larger than the truth, and the badge goes to the cheapest credit, but only when that is cheaper than the smallest pack. Pass bestValue with an id to choose another pack, or null for no badge. The packs are a radio group (arrow keys move and choose, one tab stop) with the best value pack chosen at the start, or the one in defaultValue; value and onValueChange make it controlled. The button hands the chosen pack to onSelect and the section takes no payment itself. expiry is the rule buyers ask about first and is said beside the button as a plain sentence, so Credits never expire and Credits are valid for 12 months are written alike. Under 672px every pack is a compact row with the price on the right; from there the packs are cards that share their rows through a subgrid, so credits, prices and savings line up, and the columns follow the count so no card is left alone in a row. labels translates every fixed word.

items.name: rate-card
items.title: Rate card
items.description: Metered pricing as a plain table: each resource with what is included free, then the price per unit, so developers can estimate without a calculator.
items.docs: Pass the groups (a title and rows of resource, included, rate, unit and an optional note), billing (how the product is billed, in words), checkedOn (the day the prices were checked) and the currency and locale. billing and checkedOn are required on purpose: they are the caption, and a rate card that does not say how old it is goes stale unnoticed. Included may be a number, written in the locale, or text such as 10 GB or Unlimited, and null says nothing is included. A numeric rate is written as money with up to four digits for a fraction of a cent, followed by per and the unit; 0 reads as Free, null as no extra charge, and text such as Custom is shown as written. The table is semantic, with the caption, column headers, a header row for every group and a row header for every resource. Under 672px the rows become stacked blocks that keep their column names, so nothing scrolls sideways, and explicit roles keep it a table for a screen reader in both layouts. items.name: cohort-signup
items.title: Cohort signup
items.description: The next intake of a course or programme: start date, length, price, seats left and an enrol button, with the application deadline.
items.docs: Pass the cohort (name, startsAt, weeks, schedule, price, seatsTotal, seatsTaken and deadline, and optionally priceNote, what the price is for), an action and the currency, locale and timeZone it is written in. startsAt and deadline are ISO times with an offset or a Z. The price is the biggest number in the enrolment panel. The seats are a bar with the count in words (14 of 30 left); at or below lowSeats the count turns heavy and says Only. When the seats run out the card says Full in text, the button becomes Join the waiting list (onClick is told which it was: reserve or waitlist) and a line says how the reader will be told. Once the deadline has passed the button closes and the card says Applications closed. That is judged on the reader's clock after the page has mounted, so the server never claims it and a page built ahead of time cannot go stale; pass now, the same on the server and in the browser, to pin the moment for a test or a screenshot. The action is a link when it has an href and a button when it has not, and syllabusHref adds a quiet link under it. On a wide section the facts sit beside the enrolment panel; on a narrow one they stack. The only client JavaScript is that clock; a function passed to it must come from a client component. labels translates every fixed word.

items.name: webinar-signup
items.title: Webinar signup
items.description: Register for a live session: the date in the viewer's own time zone, the speakers, what you will learn and a two-field form.
items.docs: Pass the event (title, startsAt, duration in minutes and the timeZone it is announced in), the speakers (a name, a role and an optional image; initials show until it loads), what the reader will learn, and onSubmit, which receives the name, the email and whether they want the recording, and may be async: resolve to confirm, reject to show the error and keep everything typed. items.name: rsvp-form
items.title: RSVP form
items.description: Reply to an invitation: name, yes or no, number of guests, dietary needs and a message, with a warm confirmation.
items.docs: Pass the event (name, startsAt, timeZone and place), onSubmit and, as you need them, maxGuests (the most guests one reply can bring, not counting the person replying: 2 by default, and 0 leaves the guest count out), dietary (the needs to tick), deadline and calendarHref. onSubmit receives the name, whether they are coming, the number of guests, the dietary needs and the message, and may be async: resolve to confirm, reject to show the error and keep everything typed. Yes and no are two large radio cards, one above the other and side by side only once the form is wide enough for both to hold their words; choosing no takes the guest count and the dietary needs away, so nobody answers what does not apply. Mistakes are said in words once the reader has been in a field or tried to send, and the first one takes focus. The confirmation repeats the answer in words (Sanne, we have you down as coming with 1 guest), lists the dietary needs noted, offers Add to calendar to people who are coming (a data: URL or an .ics file you supply) and has Change my answer, which reopens the form with every answer as it was and puts focus on the first field. The date is written in the event's time zone without naming it, because the guests are there. defaultStatus done with defaultValues starts on the confirmation. labels translates every fixed word, errors included.

items.name: booking-bar
items.title: Booking bar
items.description: A horizontal search bar for stays, rentals and rides: dates in one two-month calendar, guests as counters and a button, stacking into a form on a phone.
items.docs: Pass onSearch, which receives the stay (from and to), the number of nights, the adults, the children and the location when the reader searches and everything is in order, and optionally locations (a value, a label and a description), minNights, maxGuests, minDate, weekStartsOn, defaultValue and locale. Days are calendar days at midnight in the reader's own time zone; in defaultValue write them as ISO dates (2026-12-18) so a value that crosses from a Server Component never shifts with a time zone. The dates are one picker: a two-month calendar from 640px and one month below, where the stay is a band, pointing at or moving to a day previews it, days before minDate and days closer to the check-in than minNights cannot be chosen, and pressing one says why in words (Minimum stay is 2 nights.). Once a stay exists the number of nights is said in words in the field (18 Dec to 21 Dec, 3 nights). The guests are two counters in a panel, adults from one, with a limit on the total that the panel states in words. A search without dates, or with a stay shorter than the minimum, says so under the bar, marks the dates and puts focus on them. Every part is labelled and works by keyboard: arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down, Home and End in the calendar, Enter to choose, Escape to close. From 768px the parts sit in one raised bar; below it they stack as a form. defaultOpen starts the dates or the guests panel open, which is for documentation and screenshots: an open panel takes focus when the page loads. The calendar and the location list are their own files (range-calendar and location-field), built for this bar, so that every word they say to assistive technology comes from labels. labels translates every fixed word, errors included.

items.name: upgrade-prompt
items.title: Upgrade prompt
items.description: The wall a free user hits: what is locked, what the next plan unlocks, the price and a Not now that always works, with an optional usage meter.
items.docs: Pass the feature that is locked (the heading), the plan that unlocks it (a name, a price and what the price is for), what the plan adds as a list, onUpgrade and onDismiss. onDismiss is required on purpose: the panel has no way to hide itself, so there is always an exit, and calling it should show the free experience again, with focus moved to its heading, because the button that was pressed leaves with the panel. It is a labelled region, not a modal: focus is never trapped, nothing is dimmed behind it, and a screen reader hears Locked before the feature's name. description gives the two lines on what the feature does, compareHref adds the quieter Compare plans link, and usage (used, limit and a label) shows how much of the free allowance is gone as a meter with the numbers in words; once the allowance is used up the panel says so in a sentence with an icon, not in colour. A numeric price is written as money in the currency and locale you pass, with cents only when it has them. The panel needs no client JavaScript; a function passed to it needs a client component around it. labels translates every fixed word.

items.name: paywall-gate
items.title: Paywall gate
items.description: The subscribe-to-keep-reading moment: a fade over the last lines of an article, the offer, the price and a sign-in link for members.
items.docs: Pass the teaser (the last visible lines of the article, as real text), the headline of the offer, three benefits, the price with its period, the primary action and, for members, a sign-in link. remaining says why the reader sees the wall (You have read 3 of 3 free articles this month) and eyebrow adds a small badge with a lock. The teaser fades out with a CSS mask, which is a visual effect only: the words stay in the page for a screen reader and the card has a heading of its own, so the fade carries no information a reader would miss. Place the block directly under the visible paragraphs of the article. For search engines: a wall that shows crawlers more than readers reads as cloaking. Describe the article with JSON-LD that sets isAccessibleForFree to false and adds a hasPart whose cssSelector matches the gated part of the page (pass className="paywall" to this block, or name the wrapper of the content it hides), as Google's paywalled content guidance asks, and send crawlers the same teaser readers see. The action is a link when it has an href and a button when it has not; a function needs a client component around the block. A numeric price is written as money in the currency and locale you pass, and text such as Free is shown as written. labels translates Already a member? and Sign in.

items.name: call-us-section
items.title: Call us section
items.description: A phone-first contact block for businesses people ring: the number large, whether the line is open now, and a callback alternative.
items.docs: Pass the phone number, a title and, to say whether the line is answered, the hours (ranges of days with an opening and a closing time on the 24-hour clock) and the time zone the business keeps, such as Europe/Amsterdam. Open or closed is worked out on the reader's clock in that zone after the page has mounted, so the server never claims either: until then the status is an empty line of the same height. Pass now to pin it for a test or a screenshot. The status says Open now, until 17:30 or Closed, opens Monday at 08:00 in the reader's locale, with a dot and words, never colour alone. The number is a tap-to-call link sized for a thumb, made of its digits and a leading plus; its size follows the section's width and the length of the number, so it stays on one line on a phone. afterHours adds a second number that stands out, with a Use this one now tag, the moment the line closes, and alternative adds a Prefer we call you? link to a callback form. The whole week sits in a disclosure with today marked, under a heading one level below the section's own, and says which time zone it is in; defaultOpen starts it open. A range must not cross midnight: split it at 24:00. labels translates every fixed word.
